title: Street art and murals
examples: What is the main difference between a mural and graffiti?
Can you show me an example of legal street art?
How does community involvement change a piece of public art?

explain.say: Today we are looking at street art and murals.

items: Street art appears in public spaces.
It uses walls and surfaces as canvas.
It combines art with the environment.

draw.text: Street Art: Murals, Graffiti, Public Art

explain.say: A mural is a large piece of artwork painted directly onto a wall.
Graffiti is writing or drawing done on walls, often quickly.
Public art is any art placed for everyone to see in public areas.

draw.text: Public Art: Art for all to see

explain.say: Getting permission is very important for any public art project.
When the community helps plan the art, it connects with the place.

faq.q: What is the main difference between a mural and graffiti?
faq.a: A mural is usually a large, planned painting with a specific design. Graffiti often involves more spontaneous writing or tagging.
asks: Are murals always better than graffiti?

faq.q: Do all street art pieces need permission to be made?
faq.a: Legally, yes, most public art requires permission from the property owner or local council. Unauthorised work is often considered vandalism.
asks: Can I paint on a wall without asking?
What is the law about street art?

faq.q: Is public art always beautiful or meaningful?
faq.a: Public art can range greatly in meaning and beauty. Its value often comes from its context and the conversation it starts.
asks: Does public art have to be pretty?

faq.q: How does community involvement change a piece of art?
faq.a: When the community is involved, the art often reflects shared stories or local identity, making it feel more connected to the people.
asks: Does the community decide the art?

faq.q: Are there any rules for street artists?
faq.a: Rules vary by location, but generally, artists must respect private property and obtain necessary permits for large works.
asks: What rules do I follow as an artist?

facts: Murals are large-scale paintings executed on walls or other large surfaces.
Graffiti can range from simple tags to complex, elaborate pieces.
Public art is defined by its location and accessibility to the general public.
Gaining permission is a key step in creating authorized public art.

quiz.say: A detailed painting covering an entire side of a building is best described as:
quiz.why: A mural specifically refers to a large, planned painting on a wall.

wrong.0: Public art is a broad category; 'Mural' describes the specific technique of painting a wall.
wrong.1: A tag is typically just a signature or name written quickly.
wrong.3: Graffiti usually suggests quick writing rather than a large, detailed painting.

quiz.say: Art placed in a town square for everyone to see is an example of:
quiz.why: Public art simply means art meant for the general public to view in a shared space.

wrong.0: While often community-focused, 'Public Art' is the broader, more accurate term for the location.
wrong.2: A mural is a type of artwork, but 'Public Art' describes its location and purpose.
wrong.3: Graffiti describes the style of writing, not necessarily the location or intent.

quiz.say: If an artist paints a detailed picture on a wall after consulting local residents, this best shows:
quiz.why: Community involvement means the local people helped plan or contribute to the art piece.

wrong.0: The description suggests a large, thoughtful piece, not just a quick signature.
wrong.2: This suggests a spontaneous act, not a planned project with local input.
wrong.3: The mention of consulting residents implies permission and planning.
